extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors and litigators drafting or defending software-related patent claims in the U.S. (post-Alice / USPTO practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting and litigating software-related patent claims to survive Alice §101 scrutiny and obtain/enforce software patents in the U.S.; includes claim-drafting tactics, specification drafting tips, and litigation responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate Inventive Concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The key distinction: claims that reflect genuine improvements to technology (eligible) versus those that merely apply an abstract idea using generic computer components (ineligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame claims so they reflect a technological improvement (an 'inventive concept') rather than a mere application of an abstract idea with generic computer components. Emphasize how the claimed features go beyond generic execution on a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show Specific Technical Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Name specific technical benefits in claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and claim measurable technical benefits such as faster search times within a database, smaller memory requirements, more dynamic information filtering, more efficient information processing, reduced network bandwidth usage, improved security/encryption, or improved error correction. Quantify when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Structured UI Approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should require a specific GUI structure and prescribed functionality directly related to the GUI structure to solve a user-interface problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims that recite a specific graphical user interface structure and tie functionality to that structure. Emphasize how the GUI structure solves a particular user-interface technical problem (e.g., preserving look-and-feel, improving interaction efficiency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on Hardware-Software Integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the invention as a technological improvement by stating how it solves existing technical or industry problems and including details of computer architecture and software interaction with hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete details about computer architecture, specific sensors/processors/memory architectures, actuation or control mechanisms, and how software interacts with hardware. Show that the invention addresses hardware limitations or leverages hardware-specific features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Pure Method Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid claims that are pure abstract mental processes or un-tethered methods; tie methods to specific machines or transformations of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie method claims to specific machines, show data transformation into a different state, and avoid claim language that reads on human mental performance. Prefer machine-tied or technical-effect-focused claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the Technical Problem Clearly in the Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly identify the technical problem in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the technical problem the invention addresses in the written description so that claim scope and patentability can be tied to solving that problem during prosecution or litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the Solution in Technical Terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the solution in technical terms (algorithms, data structures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technical descriptions such as algorithms, data structures, and implementation details (not just high-level functional statements) to show how the invention achieves the claimed improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Flow Diagrams and Pseudocode
rubrics_metrics.description: Include flow diagrams and pseudocode in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide flow diagrams, pseudocode, and implementation-level figures to support that the solution is a technical implementation and to reduce the risk that claims are viewed as abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Why the Prior Art Was Deficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the prior art was deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document specific shortcomings of the prior art in the specification (e.g., performance, accuracy, resource usage) to support assertions that the invention provides a technical improvement over existing solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify Improvements (time, space, accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible include empirical or example metrics showing improvements (reduced runtime, lower memory usage, improved accuracy) to support eligibility and inventive-concept arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft Claims That Require Specific Computer Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims that require specific computer architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft independent/dependent claims that recite specific computer architecture details (processors, memory arrangements, data paths) rather than generic computing elements to demonstrate a technological solution and avoid §101 vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Mental-Step Language in Independent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mental-step language in independent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not draft independent claims in a manner that reads on human mental processes. Use concrete machine-oriented language and structural limitations instead of abstract, mental-step phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Dependent Claims with Hardware Specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Include dependent claims with hardware specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add dependent claims that narrow independent claims by specifying particular hardware elements, sensors, processors, memory architectures, or other physical limitations that strengthen the technological character of the claim set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Apparatus Claims with Structural Detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider apparatus claims with structural detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft apparatus or system claims that recite structural components and their interconnections or operations to provide an alternative to method claims and emphasize tangible, technical aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft Beauregard Claims for Software Products (non-transitory medium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft Beauregard claims for software products (with non-transitory medium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include claims directed to a computer-readable medium storing instructions (Beauregard claims) as another claim category; ensure the claim language ties the stored program to concrete technical effects rather than abstract functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Narrow Fallback Claims Tied to Specific Technical Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Include narrow fallback claims tied to specific technical effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft fallback claim(s) narrowly limited to particular technical effects or implementation details to preserve enforceable scope if broader claims are found ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation Strategy for §101 Challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner defending against a §101 challenge should identify technological innovations required by the claims and contend that the claims require more than generic software/computer elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In litigation, emphasize technical innovations present in the claims, argue the claims require more than generic elements, present factual evidence of technical improvements, and rely on factual questions where appropriate (e.g., Berkheimer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite and Analogize to Key Federal Circuit Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoke specific Federal Circuit cases finding similar claims eligible and distinguish from cases finding similar claims ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent such as DDR Holdings (look-and-feel preservation), Enfish (self-referential database table), McRO (specific animation rules), Berkheimer (inventive concept can be a factual question), Cellspin Soft (pleading-stage challenges), and Trading Tech (GUI for trading) to analogize to your claims and support eligibility arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Examiner Interviews and Account for Examiner/Art-Unit Variability
rubrics_metrics.description: §101 rejections generally are not applied consistently between art units and examiners; examiners may share thoughts on §101 rejections during interviews — use this opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in interviews with examiners to learn their §101 concerns, tailor claim amendments and arguments to the examiner's perspective and the art unit's practice, and document technical explanations revealed during interviews to support eligibility positions.
